analysis.one_liner: Bars meatpackers from owning, feeding, or controlling the livestock they slaughter, with co-op and small-packer exceptions.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing or vote after being introduced by a bipartisan group of four senators.
analysis.plain_summary: Large meatpackers increasingly raise or contract their own cattle and hogs instead of buying from independent farmers, a practice that lets them control the supply they bid on. This bill would have made it illegal for a packer to own, feed, or control livestock destined for its own slaughter lines, forcing packers to buy from independent producers on the open market. Producer-owned cooperatives and small producer-owned packers slaughtering under 2 percent of any livestock type were exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle and hog farmers, who would regain a fairer open market for their animals instead of competing against the packer's own captive supply. Consumers in rural areas where packer concentration squeezes both farmers and local economies also stand to benefit from a more competitive market.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for a packer to own, feed, or control livestock intended for slaughter for more than 14 days before slaughter, directly or through companies it controls [S3].
Applies to packers of hogs starting 18 months after enactment and to other livestock within roughly 180 days, giving existing integrated operations a transition period [S3].
Exempts farmer-owned cooperatives whose members supply the animals, so farmer-owned processing could grow even as corporate ownership was banned [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies that own or contract-feed cattle and hogs as a captive supply, and the large feedlot and contract-growing operations built around that system. Packers argue integration lets them guarantee quality and steady supply, efficiencies that could otherwise show up in prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large meatpacking companies using captive livestock

drawbacks.text: Packers and food-industry groups argue vertical integration lets them deliver consistent quality, manage food safety, and keep processing efficient, and that a blanket ownership ban could raise consumer costs or reduce supply reliability.

The exemptions for cooperatives and small producer-owned packers carve out exceptions that could concentrate livestock production through farmer-owned channels while locking out corporate packers, a trade-off some critics called unfair to non-farm stakeholders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For independent livestock producers, the potential gain was large: a ban on packer-owned livestock targets the main tool large packers use to depress open-market prices. The costs fall on packers' efficiency and on any consumer price effects, which packers' own studies (not in this record) dispute. The bill was short and focused, but critics noted the cooperative exemption could shift, not eliminate, vertical coordination.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee in October 1999 and never came out, dying when that Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Johnson introduced the bill on October 15, 1999, joined by Sens. Kerrey, Grassley, and Thomas as original sponsors [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day [S5].
The committee took no further action, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 106th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpackers, who kept their ability to own and contract-feed livestock rather than face a ban; independent farmers lost their chance at the market protections the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large meatpackers kept captive livestock supply

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship from the start: Sens. Johnson and Kerrey (Democrats) with Grassley and Thomas (Republicans), and its 9 later cosponsors split 7 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill would end packers' practice of owning, feeding, or controlling the animals they slaughter, which reduces their control over supply and costs. Packers' captive supply is widely blamed for depressing the prices independent farmers receive.

Cooperatives majority-owned by farmers who supply their own animals for slaughter were explicitly exempted, so farmer-owned processing channels were preserved and advantaged while corporate packers were restricted.
Packers owned by producers slaughtering under 2 percent of a livestock type were exempt, giving small producer-owned operations room to grow.

industries.industry: Large contract feedlot and hog-finishing operations
industries.note: Operations built to supply packer-owned or packer-contracted livestock would lose that business once the ownership ban took effect.
